issues.legal_issue: A rent-control law’s new mesne-profit limit does not govern an eviction suit that was pending when the new law commenced and that must continue under the repealed law.
material_facts: The eviction suit was filed under the earlier rent-control law before the new law commenced and was still pending when the new law took effect.
The tenant argued that the new law limited mesne profits for commercial premises to three times the standard rent.
The new law preserved pending suits and proceedings for continuation and disposal under the repealed law.
issues.conclusion: The new law’s mesne-profit limit did not apply to the pending suit; the suit continued under the earlier law.
issues.legal_principle: Section 32(3)(a) of the Rajasthan Rent Control Act, 2001 gives overriding effect to the savings for applications, suits, and proceedings pending when that Act commenced, requiring them to be continued and disposed of under the repealed Rajasthan Premises (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1950 as if it remained in force. Consequently, Section 20 of the 2001 Act does not govern such a pending suit.

predicates.eviction_suit_pending_at_new_law_commenc: An eviction suit was filed under the earlier rent-control regime and remained pending when a replacement rent-control law commenced.
predicates.new_law_preserves_pending_proceedings: The replacement law directs that pending suits continue and be decided under the earlier law.

issues.definition: When an eviction suit remains pending at the commencement of a replacement law that preserves pending proceedings under the earlier law, the replacement law’s mesne-profit limit does not apply.

issues.legal_issue: A tenant who admitted the area of the tenancy in an affidavit in earlier proceedings cannot later dispute that area in a challenge to mesne profits.
material_facts: In earlier proceedings between the same parties, the tenant filed an affidavit admitting the total covered and open area of the tenanted premises.
In the later proceedings concerning mesne profits, the tenant disputed the area included in the tenancy.
The court relied on the earlier affidavit in treating the tenant as estopped from taking the inconsistent position.
issues.conclusion: The tenant was estopped from disputing the area previously admitted, and the finding on the area did not warrant interference.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the principle of estoppel against taking a position inconsistent with an admission made in an affidavit in prior proceedings between the same parties. It upheld the factual finding because it was based on the record and was neither perverse nor illegal.

predicates.appeal_challenges_mesne_profit_order: A party appeals an order fixing mesne profits for premises held after an eviction decree.
predicates.prior_affidavit_admits_tenanted_area: The tenant previously filed an affidavit in proceedings between the same parties admitting the area of the tenancy.
predicates.later_position_disputes_same_area: The tenant later disputed that same area when mesne profits were determined.

issues.definition: In an appeal concerning mesne profits, a tenant who previously admitted the tenanted area in an affidavit between the same parties cannot dispute that area later.

issues.legal_issue: An appellate court may require a tenant to pay reasonable mesne profits or compensation while a stay prevents execution of an eviction decree.
material_facts: The trial court granted an eviction decree, which was confirmed on appeal.
A further appeal was pending and the eviction decree was stayed.
The landlord sought mesne profits during the continuation of the stay.
The High Court directed payment of mesne profits while the stay remained in force.
issues.conclusion: The direction to pay mesne profits or compensation during the stay was consistent with the governing law.
issues.legal_principle: Under Order XLI Rule 5 read with Section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure, an appellate court granting a stay may impose reasonable terms to compensate the decree-holder for loss caused by delayed execution. Marshall Sons & Co. (I) Ltd. v. Sahi Oretrans (P) Ltd. and Another, (1999) 2 SCC 325, recognizes the need for reasonable mesne profits when execution of a possession decree is delayed. Atma Ram Properties (P) Ltd. v. Federal Motors (P) Ltd., (2005) 1 SCC 705, holds that compensation may reflect the amount for which the premises could presently be let. State of Maharashtra v. Super Max International Pvt. Ltd. and others, (2009) 9 SCC 772, reaffirmed that view. After an eviction decree, the tenancy terminates and the landlord may receive mesne profits or compensation for loss of use.

predicates.appeal_seeks_to_continue_stay_of_evictio: An appeal concerns a request to continue a stay against execution of an eviction decree.
predicates.eviction_decree_has_been_passed: A court has granted a decree for eviction.
predicates.stay_delays_possession_and_execution: A stay prevents the decree-holder from obtaining possession and delays execution of the decree.

issues.definition: When an appeal seeks to maintain a stay that delays possession under an eviction decree, the appellate court may require reasonable mesne profits during the stay.

issues.legal_issue: The amount of mesne profits during a stay may be fixed by assessing the premises’ current letting value in light of their location, character, and rental evidence.
material_facts: The premises were in a commercial area on a main road in the heart of a city.
The High Court considered the location and the documentary record when assessing the area and value of the premises.
The standard rent had been fixed years earlier, and the eviction decree had also been in place for several years.
The Supreme Court found the factual findings supported by the record and the monthly amount fixed by the High Court just and proper.
issues.conclusion: The amount fixed by the High Court was reasonable and warranted no interference.
issues.legal_principle: Marshall Sons & Co. (I) Ltd. v. Sahi Oretrans (P) Ltd. and Another, (1999) 2 SCC 325, and Atma Ram Properties (P) Ltd. v. Federal Motors (P) Ltd., (2005) 1 SCC 705, support mesne profits or compensation based on the rent obtainable in the present market. State of Maharashtra v. Super Max International Pvt. Ltd. and others, (2009) 9 SCC 772, reaffirmed the principle. The amount depends on the circumstances of each case, including whether the property is in a village, city, or metropolitan area, its location, whether it is commercial or residential, and the prevailing rental rates for comparable letting. A factual assessment supported by the record and not shown to be perverse or illegal does not warrant appellate interference.

rule.if: appeal_challenges_mesne_profit_amount and premises_are_held_after_eviction_decree and market_rent_assessment_considers_location_and_property_character and amount_finding_is_supported_by_record

predicates.appeal_challenges_mesne_profit_amount: A party appeals the amount of mesne profits fixed for premises held after an eviction decree.
predicates.premises_are_held_after_eviction_decree: The occupant continues to hold the premises after an eviction decree.
predicates.market_rent_assessment_considers_locatio: The assessment considers the premises’ location, whether they are commercial or residential, and the rent they could presently obtain.
predicates.amount_finding_is_supported_by_record: The amount is based on material in the record and is not shown to be perverse or illegal.

issues.definition: An appellate court upholds a mesne-profit amount supported by the record when the assessment reflects the premises’ current letting value and relevant characteristics.

issues.legal_issue: A review court cannot reconsider the merits as an appellate court absent an error apparent on the face of the record.
material_facts: The tenant sought review of the order fixing mesne profits, raising the new-law cap argument and disputing the area included in the tenancy.
The High Court concluded that the new law did not govern the pending suit and that the tenant’s objection to the area was not a basis for review.
The High Court dismissed the review, and the Supreme Court upheld that decision.
issues.conclusion: The review petition was properly dismissed because the tenant had not shown an apparent error warranting review.
issues.legal_principle: The High Court applied the principle that review is not an appeal in disguise and that the reviewing court does not reassess the merits unless an error apparent on the face of the record is shown. The Supreme Court upheld that approach in light of the savings provision in Section 32 of the Rajasthan Rent Control Act, 2001 and the record concerning the tenanted area.

predicates.review_challenges_mesne_profit_order: A party seeks review of an order fixing mesne profits.
predicates.no_error_apparent_on_record: The party does not establish an error apparent on the face of the record.

issues.definition: A party seeking review of a mesne-profit order cannot obtain a fresh merits determination when no error apparent on the record is established.
